items.stem: An AI assistant tells you, "I deleted the rows." What did the model itself do?

options.text: It wrote a text request for a tool call. The client then ran it.
options.feedback: The model only produces text. A separate program, the client, decides whether to run the request and then does it.

options.text: It ran the SQL statement directly against the database.
options.feedback: The model has no connection to your database. It has only the tool description.

options.text: It asked the database for permission, and the database ran the statement.
options.feedback: The database does not take requests from the model. The client sits between them.

options.text: It logged in to your server and typed the command.
options.feedback: The model cannot log in anywhere. It can only produce the request.

items.stem: On the risky tool, where can a person stop the deletion?

options.text: After the model writes the request and before the client runs it.
options.feedback: This is the only point where the request exists as text and nothing has changed yet.

options.text: After the client runs it, by pressing undo to restore the rows.
options.feedback: Once the client runs a delete, the rows are gone. There is no undo in this setup.

options.text: While the model is still writing the request, by interrupting it.
options.feedback: The request is not complete until the model finishes it, so there is nothing yet to approve or refuse.

options.text: Nowhere, because the model decides and cannot be stopped.
options.feedback: The client decides whether to run each request, so a person can place a check there.

items.stem: A company has 6 AI applications and 8 internal systems. How many adapters does it write without a shared standard, and how many pieces does it write with MCP?

options.text: 48 adapters without a standard and 14 pieces with MCP.
options.feedback: Without a standard, every pairing needs its own adapter: 6 × 8 = 48. With MCP, each side is written once: 6 + 8 = 14.

options.text: 14 adapters without a standard and 48 pieces with MCP.
options.feedback: These are reversed. Multiplying gives the larger number, and that is the case without a standard.

options.text: 48 adapters in both cases, with or without MCP.
options.feedback: A shared standard lets each application and each system be written once, so the count is the sum of the two sides.

options.text: 8 adapters without a standard and 6 pieces with MCP.
options.feedback: These count one side only. Every application needs a connection to every system.

items.stem: Which of these stays your responsibility even when you use MCP?

options.text: Deciding whether a request to delete data should be made.
options.feedback: MCP delivers requests. Judging whether a request is a good idea stays with you.

options.text: Connecting one AI application to many systems without writing a new adapter for each.
options.feedback: This is what MCP is for. Each client and each server is written once.

options.text: Deciding how the model and the tool server format their messages.
options.feedback: MCP defines the message format, so you do not design one.

options.text: Using the same server in a different editor later.
options.feedback: Portability is one of the benefits. Any client that follows the protocol can use the server.
